note.question: Does allowing publishers to use both private marketplaces and real-time bidding create adverse selection that harms RTB-only publishers and advertisers?
note.overview: A dual-channel publisher privately observes impression quality and strategically allocates impressions between a private marketplace and real-time bidding, chooses a floor, and faces advertisers bidding in a second-price auction. The three-stage game is solved by backward induction and then tested empirically.

models.method: The paper solves the three-stage game by backward induction, derives the quality threshold and cross-publisher externality, and tests the predicted quality difference with 2019 demand-side-platform data using a three-stage sample-selection correction.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: The dual-channel publisher first commits to a quality threshold for PMP. When an impression arrives, each publisher observes its quality, chooses a channel when relevant and sets a floor price. Advertisers receive a bid request, form rational channel-level quality expectations and simultaneously bid in a second-price auction; the winner's ad is displayed and pays the applicable second-highest bid or floor. The dual-channel publisher screens its own impressions by quality before sending the residual pool to RTB.

components.label: Backward-induction equilibrium of the three-stage channel-allocation and second-price auction game
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Backward-induction equilibrium of the three-stage channel-allocation and second-price auction game. The authors solve advertiser bids first, then publisher floor prices and channel allocation, and finally the dual-channel publisher's threshold. In the resulting rational-expectations outcome, beta*=q_hat v and the equilibrium floor is proportional to expected quality, while selective routing creates adverse selection in RTB.
